routes.description: Move from an assumed fundamental reality to God-like perfection by treating unexplained nonmaximal parameters as arbitrary and reducing such arbitrariness across perfection-relevant attributes.
routes.successCriteria: Establish that relevant foundational limits require explanation, that the foundation possesses greatness or value, and that unresolved limits cannot remain in its perfection-relevant attributes.

motionBridge.description: Connect the absence of arbitrary limits in foundational greatness, power, positivity, and persistence to a perfect or quasi-perfect foundation.

centralBridges.description: Supply a defensible reason why apparently arbitrary foundational limits require further explanation.
Establish that fundamental reality possesses some greatness or value to which limits reasoning can apply.
Show that explaining a limited attribute cannot merely relocate the same arbitrariness into a deeper necessitating ground.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Specify how unexplained parameters count in comparative theory choice even when the argument is not independently conclusive.
Preserve a moderated conclusion by requiring arbitrariness to be reduced as far as the available explanations permit.

routes.description: Block the move to God-like perfection by showing that explanatory principles, foundational value, and the inference from explained limits to maximal attributes require independent comparative support.
routes.successCriteria: Show that rival theories may rationally retain explained or brute limits, that greatness or mentality is not established, or that nonarbitrariness does not entail maximal perfection.

motionBridge.description: Establish that the limits argument does not by itself discriminate decisively between a perfect foundation and relevant non-theistic or imperfect foundations.

centralBridges.description: Require assessment of unexplained limits within an all-things-considered comparison of competing theories and their virtues.
Challenge the premise that fundamental reality has value, greatness, or mentality sufficient for the perfection inference.
Preserve the possibility of a necessary or essential explanation for a nonmaximal foundational attribute.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish unexplainedness, inexplicability, and the relevant modal alternatives within the concept of arbitrariness.
Test whether the support for explaining limits equally supports rival principles with contrary theoretical consequences.

sectionSelections.title: Arbitrariness and the argument's comparative scope
sectionSelections.rationale: This issue fixes the operative concept of an arbitrary limit and determines whether the argument purports to demonstrate its conclusion or identify a comparative theoretical cost.

proSelections.proposition: A hypothesis about fundamental reality can be examined through the unexplained arbitrariness of its intrinsic limits rather than only through its capacity to produce observed effects.
An arbitrary limit is an unexplained nonmaximal degree for which reason permits greater or lesser degrees, thereby inviting an explanation of why that degree obtains.

conSelections.proposition: The argument must distinguish actual unexplainedness from inexplicability and clarify which genuine, apparent, or conceivable alternatives make a limit arbitrary.
Because a non-theistic theory may entail fundamental limits and reject the explanatory premise, the argument cannot adjudicate between theories without comparing their wider virtues and costs.

sectionSelections.title: Support for explaining fundamental limits
sectionSelections.rationale: The route from bounded foundational attributes toward an unlimited foundation depends on whether apparent irrelevant differences and explanatory practice justify extending explanation to the fundamental case.

proSelections.proposition: Apparently irrelevant differences among possible foundational limits, together with the ordinary track record of further explanations, support thinking that such limits require explanation.
If the considerations supporting the limits principle equally support a competing principle, that support is undercut unless a symmetry breaker distinguishes their applications.

conSelections.proposition: A theory's comparative simplicity and explanatory power may provide reason to expect a relevant difference supporting its foundational limit even before that difference is specified.
The inductive, abductive, intuitive, and relevant-difference support offered for the limits principle can also support rival causal principles whose consequences conflict with traditional theism.

sectionSelections.title: Foundational greatness and mentality
sectionSelections.rationale: Limits reasoning reaches perfection only if fundamental reality has a perfection-relevant degree of greatness or value, and its reach toward theism also depends on the separate issue of mentality.

proSelections.proposition: If fundamental reality has some greatness, its limits have explanations, and its greatness is not arbitrarily limited, then it is perfect in the relevant sense.
The greatness premise can receive supplementary support from independent arguments for foundational mentality and from the foundation's power to produce value.

conSelections.proposition: A mindless fundamental reality may be axiologically neutral rather than great, so establishing foundational greatness appears to require first establishing mentality.
The limits argument alone does not establish theism because it requires an additional premise or independent argument showing that the foundation is minded.

sectionSelections.title: Grounding value in the foundation
sectionSelections.rationale: This issue determines whether derivative valuable states warrant attributing value to their ultimate ground, which supplies a required premise for applying limits reasoning to greatness.

proSelections.proposition: If a value-entailing property is grounded in something, its ground is also value-entailing, because positive aspects require an antecedently valuable potential.
A foundation's capacity to produce valuable states is itself valuable because without that capacity no value could arise in the resulting sequence.

conSelections.proposition: The claim that value or greatness must be grounded in prior value or greatness faces cases in which non-great components ground a great whole and remains conceivably false.
Being a necessary condition for value does not itself make something valuable, just as necessary mathematical truths need not be valuable merely because value could not exist without them.

sectionSelections.title: Explained submaximal limits and inherited arbitrariness
sectionSelections.rationale: The decisive transition from nonarbitrariness to perfection turns on whether a submaximal limit can be explained without transferring unresolved arbitrariness into its deeper ground.

proSelections.proposition: When a grounding property necessitates one arbitrary limited outcome rather than relevant alternatives, the ground inherits that arbitrariness and still calls for explanation.
Even if deeper grounds for some limits remain open, minimizing arbitrariness supports at least a quasi-perfect foundation without arbitrary unexplained limits in its attributes.

conSelections.proposition: A foundation can have a nonmaximal but nonarbitrary degree of greatness when its limit is explained by metaphysical necessity or by its essential nature.
The arbitrariness-inheritance principle risks equivocating between unexplainedness and comparative non-difference or making God inherit the arbitrary limits of creation.
